newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish secularist Yilmaz tipped to win key vote.
newsitem.headline: Turkish secularist Yilmaz tipped to win key vote.

text.p: Turkish anti-Islamist Prime Minister Mesut Yilmaz garnered further parliamentary support on Friday, the eve of a confidence vote that his minority coalition looks likely to win.
Two MPs resigned from the opposition and a group of independents swore allegiance to Yilmaz's loose alliance of secularists from both the left and right.
Yilmaz was appointed prime minister two weeks ago to replace Necmettin Erbakan, who stepped down last month after a stormy year in office as Turkey's first Islamist leader.

"This government will be useful even if only to find a solution to lift Turkey from its trauma and deep division," conservative independent Emre Gonensay told a news conference. Three other MPs without parties said they would vote for Yilmaz.

The powerful generals, self-appointed guardians of Turkey's secularist tradition, had begun to hint at army intervention against the Islamists after months of public disputes over Erbakan's attempts to increase the profile of Islam.
Yilmaz's majority on paper is around 15 votes over the combined opposition, led by Erbakan's Islam-based Welfare Party.
The margin could be boosted by opposition conservatives staying away from parliament in quiet protest at their True Path Party leader Tansu Ciller's ties to the Islamists.
Yilmaz and his two government partners have 216 MPs. They also expect the support of 49 other left-wing deputies, two rightists and 17 of the independents in the 550-seat assembly.
Ranged against Yilmaz are 157 Islamists, eight far-rightists and 99 conservative True Path MPs, some of whom are suspected of sympathy for the government.
"The government will win the vote tomorrow by a wide margin," Zeki Cakan, a leading MP in conservative Yilmaz's Motherland Party, told a news conference.

Turkish shares, volatile in recent weeks, have calmed since free-marketeer Yilmaz was appointed. Istanbul stock exchange's general index was down slightly in mid-afternoon trading after steady gains earlier in the week.
Yilmaz has promised to introduce anti-Islamist legislation, particularly on education, before taking the country to early elections next year.
"In the coming days, a law will be delivered to parliament and preparations for elections will be included in this law," Motherland's Cakan said. He did not mention a polling day.
Yilmaz has indicated he would seek polls early in 1998 but a left-wing party that supports him wants elections sooner.
On foreign policy, the Yilmaz administration has helped to melt some of the ice with regional rival Greece in a U.S.-sponsored agreement to reduce in the Aegean Sea.
Leftist Foreign Minister Ismail Cem, a quiet intellectual, is taking much of the credit in Turkey for the accord.

Yilmaz is strongly pushing Turkey's difficult bid to join the European Union, in contrast to the Islamists whose efforts to get closer to radical Moslem nations Iran and Libya annoyed Turkey's secularists and Western allies.

Two True Path MP quit on Friday. One of them called on the party to overthrow leader Ciller, a pro-Western former foreign minister who dismayed secularists by forming a coalition with the Islamists last year.
"I hope that the colleagues I have left behind will be able to achieve the resignation of the chairwoman," resignee Demir Berberoglu said in his resignation letter.
Corruption accusations against Ciller, who became Turkey's first woman leader in 1993, have begun to resurface since she left office.
